questions.stem: A 69 year old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin is admitted with pyelonephritis and acute kidney injury. He is confused and breathing rapidly. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 88/54 mmHg and respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute. Investigations (arterial):
questions.q: Which is the most likely acid-base disturbance?
questions.e: Low pH with low HCO3- is metabolic acidosis; an anion gap of about 31 means unmeasured acid (lactate from sepsis, AKI, metformin).

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
**pH low + HCO3- low** = metabolic acidosis; calculate the gap with **(Na + K) − (HCO3- + Cl)**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gap ≈ 31: raised anion gap metabolic acidosis.

elim: pH and bicarbonate are low, not high.
The gap is (138 + 4.9) − (11 + 101) ≈ 31, well above 20.
PaCO2 is low; the CO2 is compensating, not causing the acidosis.
pH is low, so the low CO2 is compensation, not a primary alkalosis.

steps.x: **C. Raised anion gap metabolic acidosis.** Always calculate the gap in a metabolic acidosis: >20 means unmeasured acid (lactate, ketones, toxins).

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman has a 3 month history of tiredness, weight loss and dizziness on standing. Her skin creases and gums are darkly pigmented. She has no diarrhoea or vomiting. Her BP is 92/58 mmHg lying and 74/48 mmHg standing. Investigations (venous):
questions.q: Which is the most likely acid-base disturbance?
questions.e: Addison's disease (pigmentation, postural hypotension, low Na, high K) causes a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis from loss of aldosterone-driven acid excretion.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
Pigmentation, postural drop, **hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia** = Addison's.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gap ≈ 12, normal: normal anion gap metabolic acidosis.

elim: Bicarbonate is low, not high.
The gap is (128 + 5.9) − (18 + 104) ≈ 12, which is normal.
CO2 is not raised and she has no respiratory disease.
pH is low, so this is not an alkalosis.

steps.x: **B. Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis.** Normal anion gap causes: RTA type 1, diarrhoea, Addison's.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with a known gastric cancer has a 1 week history of vomiting large volumes of undigested food. He has a dry mouth and his pulse rate is 104 bpm, BP 104/66 mmHg and respiratory rate 10 breaths per minute. Investigations (arterial):
questions.q: Which is the most likely acid-base disturbance?
o: Hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation
questions.e: Prolonged vomiting from gastric outlet obstruction loses HCl, giving a hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis; hypoventilation raising CO2 partially compensates.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
Losing **stomach acid**, slow breathing, **low chloride**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: pH up, HCO3- up, CO2 up a little, chloride low.

elim: pH and bicarbonate are high, not low.
There is no acidosis.
pH is raised; the high CO2 is compensating for a primary metabolic alkalosis.
CO2 is high, not low.

steps.x: **A. Hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation.** Vomiting = hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis; the CO2 rises as compensation.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman has a 4 month history of passing large amounts of watery mucus per rectum. Rectal examination reveals a soft, velvety mass. She takes no regular medicines and has not vomited. Her arterial pH is 7.49 (7.35–7.45), HCO3- 33 mmol/L (22–26) and PaCO2 6.3 kPa (4.7–6.0).
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her acid-base disturbance?
questions.e: Raised pH and HCO3- with a mildly raised CO2 is metabolic alkalosis with compensation; a mucus-secreting rectal villous adenoma is a listed cause.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
Metabolic alkalosis with **no vomiting** and **no thiazide**, but a **velvety rectal mass** secreting mucus.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Secretory villous adenoma.

elim: Addison's gives a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, not an alkalosis.
Diarrhoea from Crohn's typically gives a normal anion gap acidosis.
CO2 is raised, not low; this is metabolic alkalosis.
RTA gives acidosis, not alkalosis.

steps.x: **E. Secretory villous adenoma.** Metabolic alkalosis causes: vomiting, secretory villous adenoma, thiazides.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman has sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness 10 days after a long-haul flight. Her right calf is swollen. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm, BP 124/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. Investigations (arterial, on air):
questions.q: Which is the most likely acid-base disturbance?
questions.e: Pulmonary embolism drives hyperventilation, lowering PaCO2 and raising pH: an acute respiratory alkalosis with normal bicarbonate.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
**pH high, CO2 low, HCO3- normal**: CO2 is driving it.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Respiratory alkalosis from a PE.

elim: Bicarbonate is normal and pH is high.
HCO3- is normal; it is the low CO2 driving the raised pH.
CO2 is low, not raised.
Type 2 needs a raised PaCO2.

steps.x: **D. Respiratory alkalosis.** Respiratory alkalosis causes: anxiety (commonest), PE, pneumonia, early aspirin, high altitude.

questions.stem: A 23 year old woman is brought to the Emergency Department by her flatmate after an argument. She is distressed, has tingling in both hands and around her mouth, and feels she cannot get enough air. Her chest is clear. Her pulse rate is 110 bpm and respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute. An arterial blood gas is taken on air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the arterial blood gas?
o: pH 7.21, PaCO2 3.1 kPa, PaO2 12.4 kPa, HCO3- 10 mmol/L
pH 7.30, PaCO2 8.0 kPa, PaO2 8.0 kPa, HCO3- 28 mmol/L
pH 7.40, PaCO2 5.2 kPa, PaO2 12.5 kPa, HCO3- 24 mmol/L
pH 7.52, PaCO2 3.1 kPa, PaO2 14.0 kPa, HCO3- 24 mmol/L
pH 7.54, PaCO2 6.4 kPa, PaO2 11.8 kPa, HCO3- 38 mmol/L
questions.e: Panic-related hyperventilation, the most common cause of respiratory alkalosis, gives low PaCO2, raised pH and high PaO2 with normal bicarbonate acutely.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' question: predict the gas before reading four sets of numbers.

clues: tingling in both hands and around her mouth
steps.x: Anxiety + **perioral tingling** + **fast breathing** + clear chest.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Blowing off CO2: low CO2, high pH, high O2.

elim: This is metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation.
This is acute respiratory acidosis from hypoventilation.
A normal gas would not explain her tingling.
This is metabolic alkalosis, as in vomiting.

steps.x: **D. pH 7.52, PaCO2 3.1 kPa, PaO2 14.0 kPa, HCO3- 24 mmol/L.** Hyperventilation: CO2 down, pH up, O2 up, bicarbonate normal acutely.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man took 60 aspirin tablets 1 hour ago. He has tinnitus, nausea and is breathing fast and deeply. He is alert. His pulse rate is 104 bpm, BP 128/78 mmHg and respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute. Investigations (arterial, on air):
questions.q: Which is the most likely acid-base disturbance?
questions.e: Salicylates stimulate the respiratory centre early, causing respiratory alkalosis; a raised anion gap metabolic acidosis follows later.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
**Early** aspirin overdose with fast breathing.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Early salicylate toxicity: respiratory alkalosis.

elim: HCO3- is normal; the change is driven by low CO2.
pH is high, and CO2 is low.
pH is raised, not low.
This develops later in salicylate poisoning; early on pH is raised.

steps.x: **E. Respiratory alkalosis.** Aspirin: respiratory alkalosis early, raised anion gap (the S of MUDPILES) metabolic acidosis later.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman with myasthenia gravis has a 2 day history of worsening weakness, difficulty swallowing and a weak cough. She is now drowsy with shallow breathing. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm, BP 134/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. Investigations (arterial):
questions.q: Which is the most likely acid-base disturbance?
o: Respiratory acidosis with complete metabolic compensation
questions.e: Neuromuscular weakness causes alveolar hypoventilation and CO2 retention; with normal bicarbonate the kidneys have not yet compensated, so it is acute.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
**Neuromuscular weakness**, shallow breathing: CO2 retention. HCO3- **normal**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Raised CO2, low pH, normal HCO3-: acute respiratory acidosis.

elim: Compensation would lower CO2, but CO2 is high and HCO3- normal.
pH is low, not high.
pH is low and bicarbonate normal: no compensation yet.
CO2 is high, not low.

steps.x: **A. Acute respiratory acidosis.** Respiratory acidosis = hypoventilation (COPD, opioids, neuromuscular weakness). Normal HCO3- = acute.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man with severe COPD attends clinic for review. He is at his usual level of breathlessness and has no new symptoms. His pulse rate is 82 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. Investigations (arterial, on air):
questions.q: Which is the most likely interpretation?
o: Respiratory acidosis with complete metabolic compensation
questions.e: Chronic CO2 retention in COPD is compensated by renal bicarbonate retention, so pH can be normal; read CO2 and HCO3- together, not pH alone.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
Stable COPD: chronic **CO2 retention** with **high HCO3-** and a normal pH.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Fully compensated respiratory acidosis.

elim: In a man with COPD, high CO2 is the primary change; the HCO3- is compensation.
Bicarbonate is high, not low.
pH is normal but CO2 and HCO3- are both abnormal.
The pH is normal, so the disturbance is compensated.

steps.x: **D. Respiratory acidosis with complete metabolic compensation.** A normal pH does not mean a normal gas; look at CO2 and HCO3-.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man is resuscitated after a 12 minute out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. He has a return of spontaneous circulation and is being bag-mask ventilated while awaiting intubation. His pulse rate is 128 bpm and BP 84/50 mmHg. Investigations (arterial):
questions.q: Which is the most likely acid-base disturbance?
questions.e: A raised CO2 (inadequate ventilation) with a low HCO3- (lactate from hypoperfusion) both lower the pH: a mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
**CO2 high** and **HCO3- low**: both pushing pH down.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Two primary problems at once.

elim: Compensation would lower CO2; here it is high.
Bicarbonate is low, so there is no alkalosis.
Compensation would raise HCO3-; here it is low.
pH is very low and CO2 high.

steps.x: **C. Mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis.** If CO2 and HCO3- move in opposite directions and pH is very abnormal, think mixed disorder.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man is found confused in his garage. He has no smell of alcohol. Urine microscopy shows envelope-shaped calcium oxalate crystals. His creatinine is rising. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute. Investigations (venous): pH 7.12 (7.35–7.45), HCO3- 8 mmol/L (22–26), anion gap 32 mmol/L (10–20). Lactate and ketones are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his acidosis?
questions.e: A raised anion gap with normal lactate and ketones, AKI and calcium oxalate crystals is ethylene glycol (antifreeze) poisoning, the E of MUDPILES.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
Raised gap with **no lactate, no ketones**, plus **oxalate crystals**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A toxic alcohol: ethylene glycol.

elim: Ketones are normal.
Diarrhoea causes a normal anion gap acidosis.
RTA gives a normal anion gap, not a gap of 32.
Lactate is normal, so this is not lactic acidosis.

steps.x: **C. Ethylene glycol ingestion.** MUDPILES: Methanol, Uraemia, DKA, Paracetamol, Iron/Isoniazid, Lactate, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman with alcohol dependence has vomited for 2 days after stopping a week-long binge and has not eaten. She has abdominal pain and is breathing deeply. She does not have diabetes. Investigations: pH 7.20 (7.35–7.45), HCO3- 11 mmol/L (22–26), anion gap 28 mmol/L (10–20), blood ketones 5.1 mmol/L (<0.6), glucose 4.6 mmol/L (4–7), lactate 1.8 mmol/L (0.5–2.2).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Raised anion gap acidosis with high ketones, normal glucose and normal lactate after a binge and starvation is alcoholic ketoacidosis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
Gap explained by **ketones**, but **normal glucose** and no diabetes.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Alcoholic ketoacidosis.

elim: She does not have diabetes and her glucose is normal.
Glucose is normal and HHS has little ketosis.
Lactate is normal.
The ketones explain the gap; nothing suggests methanol.

steps.x: **A. Alcoholic ketoacidosis.** Ketones + normal glucose + alcohol binge = alcoholic ketoacidosis.

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman with atrial fibrillation who stopped her apixaban a month ago has 6 hours of severe central abdominal pain. Her abdomen is soft with mild tenderness. Her pulse rate is 124 bpm irregular and BP 102/64 mmHg. Investigations (venous): pH 7.24 (7.35–7.45), HCO3- 13 mmol/L (22–26), anion gap 27 mmol/L (10–20), lactate 7.8 mmol/L (0.5–2.2), ketones 0.2 mmol/L (<0.6).
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her acidosis?
questions.e: Pain out of proportion to examination in AF off anticoagulation, with a raised gap explained by lactate, is lactic acidosis from mesenteric ischaemia.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.

clues: abdomen is soft with mild tenderness
steps.x: AF, **no anticoagulant**, severe pain with a **soft abdomen**, **lactate** high.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Ischaemic gut producing lactate.

elim: Ketones are normal.
That gives a normal anion gap; hers is raised.
RTA gives a normal anion gap.
There is no overdose history; lactate explains the gap.

steps.x: **C. Lactic acidosis from mesenteric ischaemia.** Raised gap with high lactate: think sepsis, shock and mesenteric ischaemia.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman with Sjögren's syndrome has muscle weakness and a recent renal stone. She has no diarrhoea and takes no medicines. Investigations: pH 7.30 (7.35–7.45), HCO3- 16 mmol/L (22–26), sodium 139 mmol/L (135–145), potassium 2.8 mmol/L (3.5–5.3), chloride 116 mmol/L (95–108). Urine pH is 6.5.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her acid-base disturbance?
questions.e: A hypokalaemic, hyperchloraemic, normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with an inappropriately alkaline urine and stones is type 1 (distal) RTA, associated with Sjögren's.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
Normal gap, **low K**, **high Cl**, stones, urine **not acidified**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Distal RTA.

elim: Addison's causes hyperkalaemia, not hypokalaemia.
Thiazides cause metabolic alkalosis, and she takes no medicines.
DKA gives a raised anion gap; hers is (139 + 2.8) − (16 + 116) ≈ 10.
Ethylene glycol gives a raised anion gap.

steps.x: **E. Renal tubular acidosis type 1.** Type 1 RTA: hypokalaemic, hyperchloraemic, normal anion gap acidosis.

questions.stem: An 82 year old man is brought from his care home with 2 days of increasing confusion. Staff say he is breathing unusually deeply. He has chronic kidney disease stage 5 and has missed two dialysis sessions. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute. His arterial pH is 7.28 (7.35–7.45), PaCO2 3.4 kPa (4.7–6.0), HCO3- 12 mmol/L (22–26) and urea 41 mmol/L (2.5–7.8).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Missed dialysis causes uraemia (the U of MUDPILES) and failure to excrete acid; pH <7.35 with low HCO3- is metabolic acidosis, presenting non-specifically with confusion and deep breathing.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: build the picture from the stem before looking at the options.
**Non-specific** confusion and deep breathing; **pH 7.28**, low HCO3-, missed dialysis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Uraemic metabolic acidosis.

elim: pH and bicarbonate are low.
His CO2 is low and he is breathing deeply, not hypoventilating.
pH is below 7.35, so this is an acidosis.
Confusion and deep breathing are explained by the acid-base disturbance.

steps.x: **B. Metabolic acidosis due to uraemia.** Presentation is often vague (confusion, altered breathing): the gas makes the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 76 year old woman with COPD is drowsy on the respiratory ward 2 hours after a junior doctor increased her oxygen to 15 L/min via a non-rebreathe mask. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm, BP 138/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 12 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99%. Her capillary glucose is 6.2 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: ABG measures pH, PaCO2 and HCO3- together, confirming the acidosis and showing CO2 is the driver: oxygen-induced hypercapnic respiratory acidosis.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what you need to know and which test answers it.
Drowsy COPD patient on **high-flow oxygen**: suspect **CO2 retention**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: ABG.

elim: A film will not show whether CO2 has risen.
Drowsiness after high-flow oxygen in COPD is CO2 narcosis until proven otherwise.
Her saturation is already known to be 99%; it says nothing about CO2.
Bicarbonate alone cannot show pH or CO2.

steps.x: **A. Arterial blood gas.** The ABG is the gold standard: pH, PaCO2 and HCO3- together.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man has had 10 days of profuse watery diarrhoea after travel to Nepal. He is tired and dizzy. His pulse rate is 102 bpm and BP 108/68 mmHg. Investigations (venous): pH 7.31 (7.35–7.45), HCO3- 17 mmol/L (22–26), sodium 137 mmol/L (135–145), potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5–5.3), chloride 112 mmol/L (95–108).
questions.q: Which is his anion gap?
questions.e: (137 + 3.1) − (17 + 112) ≈ 11 mmol/L, within the normal 10–20: bicarbonate lost in stool is replaced by chloride, a normal anion gap acidosis.

steps.x: A calculation question: write the formula down before you add anything up.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: About 11: normal gap.

elim: This leaves out potassium; the formula here is (Na + K) − (HCO3- + Cl).
Check the arithmetic: 140.1 − 129 ≈ 11.
This would be a raised gap; diarrhoea gives a normal gap.
This leaves out bicarbonate.

steps.x: **A. 11 mmol/L.** Anion gap = (Na + K) − (HCO3- + Cl), normal 10–20. Diarrhoea: normal gap, high chloride.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man with atrial fibrillation not on anticoagulation has 8 hours of severe abdominal pain. His abdomen is soft. His arterial gas shows a raised anion gap metabolic acidosis with a lactate of 6.9 mmol/L (0.5–2.2). His blood ketones and salicylate level are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation to find the cause of his acidosis?
questions.e: Once the pattern is identified, the cause is sought with targeted tests and imaging; suspected mesenteric ischaemia causing lactic acidosis needs a CT angiogram.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what you need to know and which test answers it.
Pattern known; **AF + pain with soft abdomen + lactate** suggests mesenteric ischaemia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Image the mesenteric vessels.

elim: An X-ray is insensitive for mesenteric ischaemia.
The pattern is already identified; now find the cause.
Amylase may be mildly raised but will not confirm the diagnosis.
This will not identify a source of lactate.

steps.x: **B. CT angiogram of the abdomen.** ABG gives the pattern; targeted tests and imaging find the cause.

questions.stem: A 22 year old woman with type 1 diabetes has vomited for a day and is breathing deeply and rapidly. Her capillary glucose is 26 mmol/L. Her venous pH is 7.14 (7.35–7.45), HCO3- 9 mmol/L (22–26) and anion gap 30 mmol/L (10–20). Her pulse rate is 122 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the unmeasured anion?
questions.e: The anion gap quantifies unmeasured anions; in type 1 diabetes with high glucose these are ketones, confirmed by blood ketone measurement (DKA).

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what you need to know and which test answers it.
Type 1 diabetic, **Kussmaul breathing**, raised gap.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The anion is a ketone: measure ketones.

elim: Useful to find a precipitant, but they do not identify the anion.
This matters in HHS; it does not identify the unmeasured anion.
There is no overdose history; diabetes and glucose point to ketones.
These suggest ethylene glycol, not DKA.

steps.x: **B. Blood ketones.** Anion gap = unmeasured anions; in DKA they are ketones.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman with Crohn's disease has had 8 days of profuse diarrhoea during a flare. She is weak and dizzy. Her pulse rate is 106 bpm and BP 102/64 mmHg. Her venous pH is 7.30 (7.35–7.45) and bicarbonate 16 mmol/L (22–26). Her anion gap is 13 mmol/L (10–20).
questions.q: Which other blood result is most likely?
questions.e: Diarrhoea loses bicarbonate and potassium, so chloride rises to keep the gap normal: hypokalaemic, hyperchloraemic, normal anion gap acidosis.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what you need to know and which test answers it.
Normal gap with low bicarbonate means **chloride has risen**; stool loses **potassium**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Low potassium, high chloride.

elim: Low chloride fits vomiting and alkalosis, not diarrhoea.
Hyperkalaemia points to Addison's, not diarrhoea.
Chloride must rise to keep the gap normal as bicarbonate falls.
Neither fits stool losses.

steps.x: **A. Potassium 2.9 mmol/L, chloride 115 mmol/L.** Diarrhoea: normal gap, hyperchloraemic, hypokalaemic.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man with type 1 diabetes is in the Emergency Department with DKA. His venous pH is 7.10 (7.35–7.45), blood ketones 6.0 mmol/L (<0.6) and glucose 28 mmol/L. He has received 1 litre of 0.9% saline over an hour. His potassium is 4.6 mmol/L (3.5–5.3). His pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 114/70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: The cornerstone of acid-base management is treating the cause: in DKA that is insulin, which switches off ketogenesis.

steps.x: A management question: work out the severity and the stage of treatment first.
Fluids started, potassium normal: now **switch off ketone production**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: IV fixed-rate insulin.

elim: Bicarbonate is not used in DKA; treating the cause corrects the acidosis.
His deep breathing is compensation; NIV is for hypercapnic failure.
Metformin has no role in DKA.
Basal insulin alone will not clear ketones fast enough.

steps.x: **A. Intravenous fixed-rate insulin infusion.** Treat the cause: insulin for DKA, not bicarbonate.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman with COPD has a 3 day exacerbation with purulent sputum. She is alert. Her respiratory rate is 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 84% breathing air. Her arterial gas on air: pH 7.38 (7.35–7.45), PaO2 6.9 kPa (10–13), PaCO2 6.8 kPa (4.7–6.0), HCO3- 31 mmol/L (22–26).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management of her oxygenation?
o: Controlled oxygen via Venturi mask, target 88–92%
No oxygen to avoid CO2 retention
questions.e: In COPD with chronic CO2 retention, controlled oxygen to 88–92% is first-line; NIV is added if a respiratory acidosis develops.

steps.x: A management question: work out the severity and the stage of treatment first.
Chronic CO2 retainer (**high HCO3-**), pH normal, very hypoxic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Controlled oxygen.

elim: She is alert with a normal pH; this is not needed.
NIV is for a respiratory acidosis (pH <7.35); her pH is normal.
Withholding oxygen at PaO2 6.9 kPa is dangerous.
High-flow oxygen risks worsening CO2 retention in COPD.

steps.x: **A. Controlled oxygen via Venturi mask, target 88–92%.** COPD: controlled oxygen 88–92%; NIV if pH <7.35 with high CO2.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has a 2 day history of fever and right-sided loin pain. She is confused. Her temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 126 bpm, BP 84/50 mmHg and respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute. Her venous pH is 7.24 (7.35–7.45), HCO3- 13 mmol/L (22–26) and lactate 5.6 mmol/L (0.5–2.2). Blood cultures have been taken.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Lactic acidosis from sepsis is treated by treating the cause (antibiotics) with supportive IV fluids and oxygen.

steps.x: A management question: work out the severity and the stage of treatment first.
**Septic shock** from pyelonephritis with **lactic acidosis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Antibiotics and fluids.

elim: Fomepizole treats toxic alcohol poisoning; this is lactic acidosis from sepsis.
There is no diabetes or ketosis.
Bicarbonate does not treat the cause of lactic acidosis.
Her rapid breathing is compensation, not hypercapnic failure.

steps.x: **A. Intravenous antibiotics and intravenous fluids.** Treat the cause: antibiotics for sepsis, with oxygen and IV fluids.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman with type 2 diabetes takes metformin 1 g twice daily. She has 3 days of vomiting and diarrhoea and now has an acute kidney injury with a creatinine of 310 µmol/L (45–90). Her venous pH is 7.26 (7.35–7.45), lactate 5.1 mmol/L (0.5–2.2) and anion gap 26 mmol/L (10–20). IV fluids have been started.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Increase metformin to 1 g three times daily
questions.e: Metformin can accumulate in AKI and contribute to lactic acidosis; it is stopped in metabolic acidosis.

steps.x: A management question: work out the severity and the stage of treatment first.
**Metformin** in **AKI** with **lactic acidosis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Stop it.

elim: Adding a sulfonylurea does not address the acidosis and risks hypoglycaemia.
There is no toxic alcohol ingestion.
Metformin accumulates in AKI and worsens lactic acidosis.
The priority is removing the cause.

steps.x: **E. Stop metformin.** Stop metformin in metabolic acidosis, especially with AKI.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man with alcohol dependence has vomited for 2 days after a binge and has not eaten. He is breathing deeply. His capillary glucose is 3.9 mmol/L and blood ketones 4.8 mmol/L (<0.6). His venous pH is 7.22 (7.35–7.45). His pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Intravenous fluids with thiamine and dextrose
questions.e: Alcoholic ketoacidosis is treated with IV fluids, dextrose to switch off ketogenesis, and thiamine first to prevent Wernicke's.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman took 80 aspirin tablets 6 hours ago. She is now vomiting and agitated. She was given activated charcoal on arrival. Her plasma salicylate is 640 mg/L. questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Activated charcoal is the first step; in significant salicylate toxicity with a raised anion gap acidosis, IV sodium bicarbonate alkalinises the urine to enhance elimination.

Charcoal **already given**; now **significant toxicity** with acidosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

NAC treats paracetamol, not salicylate, overdose.

She has significant toxicity with acidosis and must not be discharged.

steps.x: **D. Intravenous sodium bicarbonate.** Salicylate: charcoal first; IV bicarbonate for significant toxicity to enhance elimination.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man has a 30 minute episode of breathlessness, chest tightness and tingling fingers while waiting for a job interview. He has had similar episodes before. His pulse rate is 104 bpm, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 100% breathing air. His ECG is normal. His arterial PaCO2 is 3.3 kPa (4.7–6.0) and pH 7.50.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Anxiety-related hyperventilation is the commonest cause of respiratory alkalosis; it is managed with breathing techniques first, with a rebreathing mask reserved for severe cases.

steps.x: A management question: work out the severity and the stage of treatment first.
**Anxiety** trigger, recurrent, normal ECG, **low CO2**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Calm the breathing first.

elim: Sedation is not first-line for hyperventilation.
He is not hypoxic; oxygen does not correct low CO2.
Beta-blockers are not used for an acute attack.
A rebreathing mask is reserved for severe cases, not the first step.

steps.x: **A. Breathing techniques and reassurance.** Respiratory alkalosis from anxiety: breathing techniques first; rebreathing mask only if severe.

questions.stem: A 24 year old man is found unresponsive after taking an unknown quantity of methadone. He has pinpoint pupils. He fails to respond to two doses of naloxone. o: Intubation and ventilation in intensive care

steps.x: **pH 7.08**, **GCS 6**, opioid not reversing.

pH 7.08 with GCS 6 is life-threatening.

steps.x: **C. Intubation and ventilation in intensive care.** Severe acid-base disturbance with a reduced GCS: ICU and ventilation.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man drank antifreeze in a suicide attempt 3 hours ago. He is drowsy. His venous pH is 7.18 (7.35–7.45) with an anion gap of 30 mmol/L (10–20). Lactate and ketones are normal. He is given the specific antidote.

questions.e: Fomepizole, the antidote for ethylene glycol, inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase so the glycol is not converted to toxic acids (glycolate and oxalate).

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman with sepsis has an arterial pH of 7.29 (7.35–7.45), PaCO2 3.6 kPa (4.7–6.0) and HCO3- 14 mmol/L (22–26). A student asks how her blood has limited the fall in pH, with bicarbonate consumed and CO2 exhaled through the lungs.
questions.q: Which buffer system is mainly responsible?
questions.e: Acid-base balance depends on the bicarbonate buffer: H+ combines with HCO3- to form CO2, a volatile acid exhaled by the lungs.

steps.x: A science question about normal physiology: think of the main extracellular buffer.
**HCO3- consumed** and **CO2 exhaled**: H+ + HCO3- ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ CO2 + H2O.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The bicarbonate buffer.

elim: Haemoglobin buffers inside red cells but is not the main extracellular buffer.
Phosphate is mainly an intracellular and urinary buffer.
Proteins contribute only a small amount.
Ammonia buffers acid in the urine, not the blood.

steps.x: **B. Bicarbonate buffer system.** Bicarbonate buffer + lungs (CO2) + kidneys (HCO3-, H+).

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with long-standing COPD has an arterial pH of 7.36 (7.35–7.45), PaCO2 7.8 kPa (4.7–6.0) and HCO3- 35 mmol/L (22–26) when well. He has been a CO2 retainer for years and takes no regular antacids. He has not vomited.

o: Loss of gastric acid by vomiting
Renal retention of bicarbonate and excretion of hydrogen ions
questions.e: Chronic CO2 retention is compensated over days by the kidneys retaining bicarbonate and excreting H+, returning pH towards normal.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind what the stem describes.
**Chronic** high CO2 with a near-normal pH: slow **renal** compensation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The kidneys keep bicarbonate.

steps.x: **E. Renal retention of bicarbonate and excretion of hydrogen ions.** Respiratory problems are compensated by the kidneys (slow); metabolic problems by the lungs (fast).

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman drank methanol-contaminated spirits on holiday 18 hours ago and now has blurred vision. She is breathing deeply at 30 breaths per minute. Her arterial pH is 7.17 (7.35–7.45), HCO3- 7 mmol/L (22–26) and PaCO2 2.4 kPa (4.7–6.0).
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for her low PaCO2?
o: Direct methanol toxicity to the lungs
questions.e: Methanol (the M of MUDPILES) causes a raised anion gap metabolic acidosis; the respiratory centre drives hyperventilation to blow off CO2 and push pH back towards normal.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind what the stem describes.

clues: breathing deeply at 30 breaths per minute
steps.x: pH **low**, HCO3- **very low**, CO2 low: the CO2 is following the bicarbonate.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The lungs compensating.

elim: Her pH is low; a primary respiratory alkalosis would raise it.
Methanol damages the optic nerve, not the lungs.
pH is low, so the low CO2 cannot be the primary problem.
There is no reason to suspect PE; the CO2 fits compensation.

steps.x: **E. Respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis.** In metabolic acidosis, hyperventilation (Kussmaul breathing) blows off CO2.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man has had 10 days of persistent vomiting from gastric outlet obstruction. He is clinically dehydrated. His arterial pH is 7.55 (7.35–7.45), HCO3- 40 mmol/L (22–26), chloride 80 mmol/L (95–108) and potassium 2.7 mmol/L (3.5–5.3). His urine pH is 5.5 despite the alkalosis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason the alkalosis is maintained?
o: Excess bicarbonate secretion by the pancreas
Increased renal chloride reabsorption causing acidosis
Volume depletion driving renal bicarbonate retention
questions.e: Vomiting loses HCl; the resulting volume and chloride depletion drives the kidneys to retain bicarbonate (paradoxical aciduria), worsening and maintaining the alkalosis.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind what the stem describes.

clues: urine pH is 5.5 despite the alkalosis
steps.x: **Dehydrated**, **low chloride**, and an **acid urine** despite alkalosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The kidneys are holding onto bicarbonate to defend volume.

elim: Pancreatic bicarbonate is lost in diarrhoea, not retained.
Compensation for alkalosis is hypoventilation, not hyperventilation.
There is no acidosis.
Aldosterone is raised secondarily from volume loss; there is no primary adrenal disease.

steps.x: **E. Volume depletion driving renal bicarbonate retention.** Vomiting: HCl loss starts it; volume depletion and renal bicarbonate retention maintain it.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman develops headache and breathlessness on the second day of a trek at 4500 metres. She is otherwise well. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. A portable blood gas shows a raised pH and low PaCO2 with a normal bicarbonate.
